analysis.one_liner: Requires agencies to repeal two regulations for every significant new one and caps total regulatory costs.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved: introduced June 1, 2020 by Sen. Kelly Loeffler with no cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Homeland Security committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law a 'two-for-one' rule: an agency could not issue any significant new regulation — one costing $100 million or more, or materially affecting health, safety, or the environment — unless it repealed two existing regulations to offset the cost. It would also give the White House budget office (OMB) an annual 'regulatory budget' capping the total cost agencies are allowed to impose, with a default cap of zero, and create task forces in every agency charged with reviewing every regulation for repeal within five years. The bill was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated businesses, especially large firms in energy, manufacturing, and finance, would save compliance costs and gain influence over which existing rules get repealed to make room for new ones. The mechanism counts the cost of rules on regulated parties but gives no binding weight to the benefits those rules deliver to the public.

how_it_helps.text: An agency could not issue a significant new regulation unless it identified at least two deregulatory actions to offset its cost, and the head of the agency must issue them on the same schedule where feasible [S3].
OMB must set an annual Federal Regulatory Budget specifying the net allowable increase in regulatory costs for each agency, and if OMB sets nothing the allowable increase defaults to zero [S3].

Each agency would install a Regulatory Reform Officer and a task force that must review every existing regulation within five years and recommend repeal, replacement, or modification, prioritizing rules estimated to eliminate jobs or impose costs exceeding benefits [S2].

The bill would give statutory authority to the existing executive order prohibiting agencies from issuing a new regulation with an economic impact of at least $100 million without identifying two regulations for repeal to offset the cost [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost of weaker protections. Repeals forced by the offset requirement would come from the stock of rules covering clean air and water, workplace safety, consumer and financial protection, and public health — rules whose benefits accrue broadly to the public while their costs fall on specific regulated firms. The bill's cost accounting measures compliance costs, not the benefits the public loses when a rule is repealed [S3].

drawbacks.text: The offset requirement applies to any significant regulatory action, including ones that 'adversely affect in a material way... public health or safety' or the environment — meaning a new clean-air or food-safety rule could be blocked unless two other protections are repealed [S3].

The bill defines regulatory 'costs' as costs to regulated parties and cost savings as the cost eliminated by repeal; it establishes no mechanism that weighs the benefits rules deliver to the public, so a rule with benefits far exceeding its costs still counts purely as a cost to be offset [S3].

OMB's regulatory budget defaults to zero if the Director sets no number, so a hostile administration could freeze essentially all new significant rulemaking, including rulemakings Congress has required by statute — though the bill excepts actions 'otherwise required by law' from the offset requirement [S3].

The strongest case for the bill, which an honest supporter would acknowledge comes at a cost: regulations accumulate over decades, some become outdated, and supporters argue a cost cap forces agencies to prioritize and cut rules whose costs exceed their benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's transparency provisions — public task force websites, published meeting minutes and comments — are real but minor. Its core mechanism, the two-for-one offset and the zero-default regulatory budget, would make it structurally harder to issue any major health, safety, environmental, or financial protection regardless of how large its benefits were, because costs to industry are counted and benefits to the public are not. The design largely locks in deregulation rather than improving the quality of rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, without a hearing or vote, until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Kelly Loeffler introduced the bill on June 1, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S1].
The bill attracted no cosponsors in either party [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2021, and the bill expired in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial protections are better off that the bill never became law, since it would have made new protections much harder to issue. Regulated industries lose the statutory lock-in of a two-for-one deregulation mandate, though the same policy already operated by executive order.

for.name: Sen. Kelly Loeffler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made its sole sponsor; no cosponsors joined

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup; the bill received no action after referral and expired at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had a single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan breakdown exists in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have saved these firms compliance costs and made new protective regulation conditional on repealing old protections. The public benefit of the rules being repealed is not counted in the bill's cost accounting, so the industry's gain comes at the public's expense.

The bill would have expanded OMB's control over every agency's rulemaking through the regulatory budget and offset requirements, while adding task forces and reporting duties. It would shift rulemaking power from agencies toward the White House budget office.
